[] That’s a very good question, Teresa, and it touches on something that’s as much about personal taste and life experience as it is about the shows themselves. For some viewers, foreign TV can feel fresh because it often comes from a completely different cultural lens—different humor, different pacing, maybe unusual plot structures or emotional tones that they don’t get in the kind of programming they’re used to. People who like to travel, study other languages, or learn about other customs may find foreign stories exciting simply because they’re getting a glimpse into a world they wouldn’t otherwise experience.

There’s also the appeal of novelty. Even everyday scenes from another country—what their homes look like, what they eat for breakfast, how they greet one another—can feel special and eye-opening to someone who’s curious about life elsewhere. For example, a police drama from the UK might approach crime-solving in a much slower, more dialogue-heavy way than the sharper, fast-paced style of an American show. That difference can be intriguing for certain audiences.

That being said, there’s a lot of comfort and depth in local programming that’s easy to miss when you’re chasing what’s exotic. Our own shows tend to reflect the social cues, shared references, and rhythms we grew up with. They speak the same cultural ‘language,’ so to speak, and can create that warm sense of recognition you can’t quite get from someone else’s storytelling traditions. Local productions might also tackle community-specific issues or values that resonate more closely with our own lives.

So while foreign TV might open up new worlds for some people, others feel more enriched, more truly “seen,” by the stories told right here at home. Both can be worthwhile—just in different ways. It all depends on whether someone is seeking familiarity and shared heritage, or the excitement of something unfamiliar.
